newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT-Australia bonds to consolidate heady run.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Australia bonds to consolidate heady run.

text.p: *Australian debt futures are set for a consolidation period after the heady run which took the 10-year yield below 7.0 percent and saw the U.S. spread dip below 50 b.p. on Monday.
*Q1 dwelling commencements due at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT), but focus on a raft of U.S. indicators later on Tuesday.

Australian bond futures look set for a period of consolidation after their recent heady run which took the 10-year yield below 7.0 percent and saw the spread to the U.S. dip briefly below 50 basis points on Monday.
The September 10-year bond futures contract ended SYCOM at 92.980, up from Monday's 92.970 pit close and after touching a high of 93.005.

The now expired 10-year June position spiked to a 3-1/4 year high of 93.090 during Monday's close-out, although for September, which is trading at a small discount, it needs to breach the market's previous peak of 93.015 set last December.
Analysts expect the September contract to hold a 92.950 to 93.020 range for now and as a prelude to a further advance to a target of 93.180.

The market has more or less priced in the expectation of a further 50 basis point cut in official interest rates, but until the Reserve Bank takes such action price gains from here could be a struggle, analysts said. The RBA board meets on July 1.
Adding to the dilemma is the absence of any major data for some two weeks, leaving the market vulnerable to moves in the U.S., although they have been positive in recent days.

U.S. Treasuries ended firm on Monday, continuing Friday's PPI-led rally, but turnover was light ahead of a raft of data later on Tuesday. These comprise CPI, housing starts, industrial production and capacity utilisation for the May period.

Locally, first quarter dwelling commencements are due at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT) and are forecast to rise 5.0 percent after the 5.9 percent increase in the December quarter, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
However, the data is seen as extremely old and will not add anything to the view that the housing sector is one of the few areas in the economy showing any signs of strength.
